newsitem.title: UK: Iraq schedules lower Kirkuk exports in Jan - trade.
newsitem.headline: Iraq schedules lower Kirkuk exports in Jan - trade.

text.p: Iraq in January is planning to export about 260,000 barrels per day of Kirkuk blend crude from Turkey's Mediterranean pipeline outlet at Ceyhan, some 75,000 bpd less than it sold in the second half of December, oil trading sources said on Friday.

Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) has scheduled nine cargoes totalling about eight million barrels, or 260,000 bpd, for January from Ceyhan, traders with a copy of SOMO's export programme said.

SOMO exported 674,000 tonnes, or 335,000 bpd in five shipments from Ceyhan in the second half of December after Turkish refiner Tupras on December 17 took title to the first Iraqi exports in six years.
Iraq, under agreement with the United Nations, is obliged to export the majority of crude from Ceyhan with the remainder from its Gulf terminal Mina al-Bakr.
Al-Bakr sales of Basrah Light are believed so far to have been limited to a pair of two-million barrel cargoes under the ownership of U.S. refiner Coastal and U.S. trader Bayoil.
That left exports from the Gulf terminal at about 260,000 bpd on average for the second half of December.
Total Iraqi liftings for the second half of December therefore were just under 600,000 bpd, traders calculate.
SOMO's Basrah Light export schedule for December was not immediately available. Japan's Mitsubishi already has fixed a tanker to load under a contract for five Japanese companies.
Italian Agip became the latest Iraqi customer with a 120,000 tonne cargo loaded at the end of December aboard the tanker Eco Africa.
Other Kirkuk buyers in December were France's Elf with 120,000 tonnes, Spain's Repsol with 140,000 tonnes and Dutch trader Trafigura with a 140,000 tonne cargo for Romania, traders said.
Austrian OMV is next in line and has been given the go-ahead to load a 95,000 tonne cargo at the weekend from Ceyhan.
The U.N.'s oil-for-food exchange allows Iraqi exports worth $2 billion over six months but permits no more than $1 billion in the first three months.
The U.N. has approved 21 SOMO export contracts for a total of just over 500,000 bpd.
With oil prices running near six-year highs Baghdad has been in danger of exceeding the ceiling.

Traders said that as a precaution SOMO has given notice to a handful of customers to lengthen their three month contracts. It may also have renegotiated lower volumes for two or three others to keep a cap on export proceeds, traders said.
In one case Agip, originally expected by industry sources to take 20,000 bpd, was approved by the U.N. for a 10,000 bpd contract, oil traders said.
